utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Andras Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's a witness who's already given evidence in these proceedings, so there'll be no need for him to take the declaration again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask at this time, while we're waiting for the witness to be brought into the chamber, if three exhibit numbers could be assigned to three separate binders of exhibits that will be given. The first is to the expert report itself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P486.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next is a two-part exhibit, Your Honour. It's the database which underlies the report. And the Prosecution is providing both a hard copy as well as an electronic, searchable copy of that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, there's a binder of four different exhibits that will be used during the course of the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'm reminded by Ms. Wee: After speaking with the legal officers of the Chamber, it was agreed that we would provide only one hard copy of the entire database and we'd provide three electronic copies. If the Chamber would like additional hard copies, of course we can provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll let you know if we do, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, in fact you've already taken the declaration in these proceedings when you gave evidence before. You are, of course, still subject to it. If you'd like now to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, the last time you testified, you gave an account of your educational and professional background. Could I ask you to begin your testimony here this morning by amplifying or adding to your previous testimony with respect to particular qualifications you have with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can add that I specialised in the history of the Balkans in my undergraduate training in history at the University of Chicago, wrote my BA thesis on Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Congress of Berlin. More specifically, over the past ten years, I've written extensively on cultural history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the subject of the destruction of cultural heritage during the recent wars. I've been invited to present papers at a number of international conferences, and I have, in addition to the Tribunal, given presentations before US congressional committees and other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would note, for the record, that Mr. Riedlmayer's full resume or curriculum vitae was Prosecution Exhibit 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I could draw your attention to the period between 1992 and 1996, did you become aware of reports coming from Bosnia indicating that there was some large-scale destruction of cultural and religious property?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise briefly the sources of that information and what the information was.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Information in general came from news reports, from publications of international bodies such as the Council of Europe, and from reports by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And more recently, were you commissioned by the Office of the Prosecutor to do a comprehensive study of the destruction of cultural and religious property, of Muslim and Catholic property, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please summarise the parameters of that report.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Following the presentation of my evidence on Kosovo, I was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor if I would be willing to conduct a similar study for Bosnia. The parameters were to look at the destruction of the cultural and religious heritage of non-Serb communities in at least 15 and up to 19 municipalities in Bosnia. In order to do this, I needed to do some field research in Bosnia for which the Office -- for which the Tribunal provided transportation and other facilities. I spent time in Bosnia in July of last year, covered 4.600 kilometres, and saw more than 230 sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the monitor in front of you. You should see displayed there a page from your report listing 19 municipalities, that report being identified now as Prosecution Exhibit 486. Are those the 19 municipalities that you visited during your mission last July?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 486. And my question to you: Is this the report that resulted from your study of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, underlying this report -- thank you. Underlying this report, did you create a database to record the information that you collected during your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 487.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have a copy to show you. Was that printed on CD-ROMs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it was printed on CD-ROMs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And will you be using that during the course of your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was a copy made of the database that you will use during your testimony --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- was a copy made -- several copies of that database made with your assistance?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to visiting sites yourself, were there other sources of information you used in creating the report that you've -- we've just tendered?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, there were. And they are described in annexes to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please summarise those sources for us, or the types of sources.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The types of sources, in addition to my own field research, included the Roman Catholic and Islamic religious communities, which had done some of their own documentation on destruction of their houses of worship and other sites. In addition to that -- that was at the Bosnia level. In addition to that, the local communities had often collected documentation, photographs, and other materials, which we were able to draw on. Also, the Council of Europe, to which I referred earlier, had sent a mission to Bosnia in 1997/1998 to examine heritage sites with a view to identifying priorities for restoration after the war, and they collected a lot of photographic material which was made available to me. The Institute for the Protection of Monuments of Bosnia had done some documentation since the end of the war, despite their limited resources, and they were in particular able to provide me with pre-war photographs of some of the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you estimate for the Chamber, what percentage of your report is based upon your personal observations during your visit to Bosnia and what proportion of your report is based upon the work of other organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Approximately three-fifths of the entries, 60 per cent, are based on personal site visits, about 40 per cent on information from other reliable sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you explain your methodology or the approach you took to locating destroyed sites of cultural and religious property.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The methodology was as follows: Before going to Bosnia, I perused all available published and unpublished information to identify in each municipality a list of sites that might be useful to look at. In addition, I made contact with the local religious communities and with the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in order to secure people who knew these sites and who would be able to guide me to particular locations. This was particularly useful in the case of sites where the structure had been completely destroyed and where locating it otherwise would have been very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you visited these sites, did you have some assessment labelling or some assessment criteria that you applied to what you found there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I used the same criteria for assessment that I used in my Kosovo study; essentially, a five-step series of damage scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to simply list them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. One is "undamaged"; two would be "lightly damaged," which is any structure that had not suffered significant structural damage to its main structure. So the top of the steeple could be shot off, but if the main structure was okay, it was lightly damaged. "Heavily damaged" is any structure that had suffered significant impairment of its principal elements. "Almost destroyed" is a structure that still had some identifiable parts remaining above ground but was essentially damaged beyond repair. And "completely destroyed" means just that, a site that had been completely levelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, of the 19 municipalities that you visited, can you estimate for the Chamber how many of the sites that you set out to find you were able to find.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In most of the municipalities, we were able to visit the vast majority of sites. In a few municipalities, such as Visegrad, time constraints and the site -- state of the roads made it impossible to visit all of them. But in virtually every municipality, we -- we have representation of the majority of sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you to summarise your findings with respect to Muslim religious and cultural property, could I ask you to describe the different types of buildings that you set out to examine, and describe what the function of those buildings were.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslim cultural property tended to include, first of all, mosques, which were used for daily and weekly communal prayers. Then there were Dervish Lodges, which were the meeting places for rituals of the Sufi lay brotherhoods. Then in addition, there were Qur'an schools, or mektebs, which were also often used for communal worship. And finally, Muslim religious libraries and communal archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could ask you now to focus on --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: And shrines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could ask you to focus on mosques alone in the 19 municipalities, approximately how many mosques did you -- or mosque sites did you visit during your -- your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: We documented 277 mosques in the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And of those 277 mosques, how many were undamaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to -- to describe your findings, your general findings, with respect to the other buildings that you've described for us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, of the mosques that we looked at, 92 per cent were found to be heavily damaged or almost entirely destroyed. Of the 71 mosques that were historic buildings and under legal protection before the war, 93 per cent were either heavily damaged or entirely destroyed. A similar number of the shrines and Dervish Lodges were also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've said that 93 per cent or -- I'm sorry, 71 of the buildings were under some form of legal protection. Can you summarise the types of legal protection that these -- that was applied to these different sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as in most places, there was an official body called the Institute for the Protection of Monuments, which proposed buildings of particular historic, architectonic, or cultural importance for legal protection. The legal protection was then extended through legislation and sites were categorised according to whether they were of national, regional, or local importance. The protection in effect meant that alterations to these buildings were prohibited without the express approval of the competent government bodies and that these sites then received some state support for restoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to describe in general terms your findings. When you went to some of these sites, what did you find? Did you find the remains of buildings, or did you find the -- the remains of these buildings removed from some of the sites? Can you give us some general idea about what you found when you went to the sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In the majority of sites that we visited which were located in what is now Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serb-controlled part of Bosnia, the mosques and other Islamic sites had been severely damaged or destroyed. The destroyed buildings in many cases had been not only burnt or blown up but the ruins had been bulldozed and the rubble removed from the site. One could tell that the building had been there often only by looking carefully for traces of foundations, and in a few cases even the foundations had been excavated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask you to turn your attention in a summary way to your findings with respect to property belonging to the Catholic community of Bosnia-Herzegovina and describe your findings there generally.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Catholic community in Bosnia-Herzegovina is largely co-extensive with the Bosnian Croat community. It is numerically much smaller than either the Orthodox or the Muslim community, and therefore the number of monuments is correspondingly smaller. The survey covered 57 Catholic churches in the 19 municipalities visited, of which none were undamaged and only 14 were lightly damaged, approximately a quarter of them. The lightly damaged churches were largely located in territory held by Bosnian government forces during the war, or in some cases were churches that were under construction at the time the war broke out. Many of the Catholic churches were -- had been razed to the ground and the construction materials removed from the site. In many places, this occurred in locations where the Catholic church was in the immediate vicinity of an Orthodox church which stood undamaged. Of the 57 Roman Catholic churches, three-quarters were either heavily damaged or totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the specifications of the study you were asked to undertake by the Office of the Prosecutor, did it ask you to go visit every Serbian Orthodox church in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was limited to property belonging to the Muslim community and the Catholic community.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask you to turn your attention to your general findings with respect to archives and libraries in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In addition to the houses of worship, I also looked at the fate of archives and libraries, particularly those belonging to the religious communities, and found that in 13 of the 19 municipalities surveyed, the local representatives of the Islamic community had reported that community religious archives had been either confiscated or destroyed by the local Serb authorities or Serb forces. In a number of these municipalities, there were also collections of Islamic religious books and ancient manuscripts which had also been destroyed. Similarly, in the case of the Roman Catholic communities, there were several reports of the confiscation or destruction of religious archives and religious libraries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you familiar with what types of records would have been kept in the archives, first of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The archives of the Muslim community were of significance, primarily because they contained the records of the vakuf, the religious endowments, which support the activities of the Muslim community, so these are property deeds and other records pertaining to these. Both the records of the Islamic and the Catholic community would contain the historical data for members of the community. In the case, for example, of the Catholic community, there would be baptismal register, registers of marriages and burials from the parish. You have to consider that in Bosnia as much as -- as in many other places in Europe, civil registration of births and marriages is a relatively recent innovation, and therefore the history of the community is often tied up with these religious archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now ask you to turn your attention to the Institute of Oriental Studies in Sarajevo. Can I ask you to summarise your findings with respect to that building.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The destruction of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Sarajevo, which according to numerous eyewitness reports was shelled and burned on the night of 17 May 1992, was probably the single largest loss of archival materials in Bosnia. The Institute of Oriental Studies held the former Ottoman provincial archives with more than 200.000 documents. It also held cadastral registers, which recorded land holdings in Bosnia at the end of the Ottoman rule in the nineteenth century, and the country's richest collection of Islamic manuscripts, the record of more than 500 years of Bosnian Muslim cultural history.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was that a one-of-a-kind collection?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was any of it able to be retrieved after the building was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Virtually none of the collection was saved. It burned in its entirety. There had been plans to evacuate it to shelters, but it was early in the war and an alternative location could not be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask you to draw your attention to the National Library in Sarajevo. Can you describe your findings regarding that building.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The National Library is in the centre of the old town in Sarajevo, at the bottom of the valley. It's located in the former Austro-Hungarian era city hall and therefore still referred to as Vijecnica town hall by Sarajevans. It had been the National Library since World War II and was to Bosnia what the British Library is in respect to Britain; it was the library of record. On the 25th of August, shortly after nightfall, it was bombarded from multiple locations, from the Bosnian Serb army lines overlooking Sarajevo. Eyewitnesses described that it was hit by more than 40 incendiary shells, which caused intense fire. The fire brigade -- and I talked to members of the fire brigade that were called out -- found itself under fire with anti-personnel weapons, such as heavy machine-guns. The city water supply had been cut off just prior to the shelling, and in short, the building burned for nearly three days and close to 90 per cent of the collection was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What quantity of books were destroyed in that fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The estimate is close to one and a half million volumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to -- to speak to a certain -- a few particular sites that you visited. Before I draw your attention to the first site, I'm going to ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 488, tab 1, and ask you if you recognise what this chart is. It's a chart including some pictures and some summary information.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is that document?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a -- this document is simply a selection of photographs from the database.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you assist members of the Office of the Prosecutor in compiling that summary list?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I helped select them, and I provided the images for the display.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard evidence about the destruction of religious property in Janja and Bijeljina. Could I draw your attention to the Atik mosque in Janja, and could I ask you to summarise your findings with respect to that mosque.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a pre-war photo of the Atik mosque or old mosque in the centre of Janja. I obtained in the photo from the president of the Medzlis of the Islamic community of Janja during my visit there. Next, please. This is a photo taken the morning after it was blown up in April of 1993. You can see a bulldozer at right working on clearing the ruins. You can see that the surrounding buildings are completely intact. You can also see by comparison with the previous image that the top of the tree in front has been blown off by the blast. You can also see that the site has not been roped off as a crime scene. The destruction is continuing unimpeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you attempt to ascertain from any documentation whether there was conflict in the town of Janja during the time that the mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: According to both the informants I interviewed and press accounts of the period, Janja was securely under the control of Serb forces since the beginning of the war. There was no fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see the next photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is the photo I took at the site. When I visited, a new mosque was under construction on the site of the old destroyed mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now ask you to look at this photograph. Do you recognise the mosque depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Dzedid mosque, or new mosque, in Janja. It's a few hundred metres away. It's a pre-war photo from a publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we see the next photo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe what's in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a photograph I took. It's just the bare foundations of the same mosque. It was destroyed the month after the old mosque was destroyed, according to the local informants I interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just so perhaps the record is clear, I would note for the record that I am moving down the photographs in the same order that they are referred to in the summary, so should anybody wish to compare Dr. -- or Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony against the summary, in future time. I'm going to ask that a video now be played. I'm going to ask you to take a look at the screen in front of you. I'd ask the usher perhaps to check whether there has been to be any adjustment to the monitor to see that video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what we are seeing, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, what you are seeing is some footage taken by an ITN news camera team, with Gaby Rado of the British ITN network. What you're seeing is the clearing of the remains of the Atik mosque in the centre of Bijeljina. And what you saw in the video briefly was people going about their business. There was no fighting going on in Bijeljina. You can see in addition to the earth-moving equipment busily moving up and down, a number of people wearing Bosnian Serb army uniforms and civilians walking past the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We're finished with the video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This was -- just to briefly recap, this happened in March of 1993, when five mosques in Bijeljina were destroyed in a single night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to the municipality of Brcko. I'd ask that you look at the next photo and tell us, do you recognise what's in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph of the Savska mosque in Brcko. It is a 250-year-old mosque, the oldest in Brcko. Please note just to the right of the mosque the beginning of a steel bridge. If you go to the next photo, you can see the same steel bridge and the empty site of the Savska mosque. According to the local Islamic community, the Savska mosque was destroyed in the summer of 1992, the very foundations dug up, and the rubble trucked outside of town to a site which was also a mass grave, into which the remains of a large number of Brcko's Muslim inhabitants had been thrown, and the rubble of the mosque was deposited on top of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this one of the buildings that enjoyed legal protection, as you've described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it was a listed monument. You can see in the little window on top of the screen, you can see that the foundations had been dug up. There's a big depression still on the ground; but otherwise, all traces of the mosque have been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to the municipality of Kotor Varos and ask you to look at the following photograph. Do you recognise the mosque depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque in the village of Hanifici, just outside of Kotor Varos, a photo taken before the war from a publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you recognise the picture that is appearing now on the right-hand portion of the screen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, on the right-hand portion of the screen is a photograph I took of the mosque. You can tell by looking at the mosque, first of all, that the roof is missing and the minaret is missing. You can also see marks of soot above the window. The interior of the mosque has been completely burned out. To orient you, the little projection that you see is on the right of the pre-war photo. It's actually a prayer niche, pointing towards Mecca. The minaret has been destroyed by explosives, and you can tell that if you look more closely, as I did, by the fact that the material is splayed out. This is a modern structure with reinforced concrete, and the metal bars are bent outwards in a very characteristic fashion. Not only was the mosque burnt out, but according to the secretary of the Islamic community who took me to the site, a number of residents of the village had taken shelter in the mosque, and they were burnt alive in the mosque when it was burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you described the damage that you found on the mosque. During your examination of this mosque, did you see any evidence of bullet pockmarks or evidence of small arms fire on the walls of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: None whatsoever. There clearly had been no fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to a mosque in the Foca municipality. Do you recognise this mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the Aladza Dzamija or multicoloured mosque in Foca. Built in 1550, it was considered one of the jewels of Balkan Muslim architecture. It was in the centre of the old town of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did this particular building enjoy legal protection?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe what you found when you visited the site in the course of this study.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The mosque had been completely demolished, according to eyewitnesses, by explosives. I have a series of photographs taken in 1996 at my behest by a graduate student, and they show explosive damage to the surrounding buildings. It's clear that the destruction had been the result of an explosion. You can see the white marks all around the foundations of the mosque. The circular trace in the front is the remains of the marble ablution fountain. Remains of the rubble of the mosque were discovered after the war in the nearby Ceotina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when to the best that you were able to tell was this particular mosque destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: According to eyewitnesses, the mosque was destroyed in 1992, after the occupation of the town by Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard some substantial evidence with respect to the Zvornik municipality. I'm going to draw your attention to several sites there and ask you to describe your findings with respect to these sites. I'd ask you to look at the picture on the screen now before you. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. It's the Dervish Lodge, or tekke, at Divic, a village just south of Zvornik. The photo comes from a 1989 illustrated magazine and shows a religious ceremony at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at this photograph and tell us, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photograph I took July last year. It's the foundations of the shrine. You can see the scale of it by the people standing in the background. The red truck is parked on top of the tombs of the two holy men who were the focus of the shrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the mosque at the same village of Divic, a pre-war photograph from the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a Serbian Orthodox church build on the site of the destroyed mosque. Before the war, the village had an almost entirely Bosnian Muslim population. After the war, it was renamed Sveti Stefan, or St. Stevens, and the church was built on the site, despite the protests of the Islamic community, which sued in the Human Rights Chamber to try to recover its rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That particular suit that you've just referred to, was there any dispute with respect to the facts of this particular mosque about the impropriety of building this church on the site of the destroyed mosque? Was there any dispute regarding those facts, that that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The destruction was not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the next mosque.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the Zamlaz mosque in Zvornik. It was the oldest surviving mosque in Zvornik, about 200 years old. This is a photo taken before the war in the late 1970s. I draw your attention to the modern building at the right of the picture with the characteristic dark stripes next to the windows. Next, please. This is a photograph taken after the war. Not only has the mosque been destroyed - you can see the same pre-war structure to the right of it - but on the site of the mosque a four-storey modern apartment building is under construction. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The finished building which stood on the site when I visited last summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you speak to the local Imam regarding when this mosque was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The person who showed me the site, which I would not have found otherwise, was the Imam of the main mosque in Zvornik, now living in exile in Tuzla. And he described how the mosque was destroyed and bulldozed in the spring of 1992, following the occupation of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is responsible for the construction that is now taking place on top of what was the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The construction is being carried out by a local private company, which is connected, apparently, with the current Municipality of Zvornik, which is run by Bosnian Serbs. The Islamic community protested the construction, and the Republika Srpska authorities in their response claim that under the old Yugoslav law, which had expropriated village's properties, the Islamic community had rights to the use of the site as long as the mosque existed, but since the mosque no longer existed, their contention was that the rights of the Islamic community to the site had been extinguished. The Human Rights Chamber found otherwise and ordered that the Islamic community be provided with compensation and possibly another site. Nothing has occurred since then, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What Human Rights Chamber is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Human Rights Chamber of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was established under the Dayton Accords as a body with a mixed local and international membership to adjudicate cases involving human rights in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution is in possession of that decision. It was not our intention to tender it, but should the Chamber wish to see those documents, we are in a position to provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now draw your attention to the village of Kozluk in Zvornik. Did you visit that village in the course of your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe what you found there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Kozluk is located just north of Zvornik, and in the centre of the village, there's a large open space where the mosque once stood. The site since the war has been used as a rubbish dump and as parking for busses. Quite recently, just before my visit, the rubbish had been cleared. These are two photographs from the year before, from 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe which of the two photographs is the one that you took.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Neither. I have a third one, which I didn't include. But I can identify the site, having visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us the approximately dates of these photographs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. They're 2000 and 2001, taken from opposite sides of the square.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to locate a photograph of the mosque as it stood before it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. I talked to people from Kozluk now living in exile, and they said they had to leave in such a hurry when they were expelled that they were not able to take possessions with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to the municipality of Nevesinje and ask you to identify the photograph on the screen before you now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Nevesinje is a municipality in the south, in Herzegovina, to the east of the Mostar, and this is the Sarajeva [phoen] Dzamija or the mosque of Sultan Bajezid, the saint, built more than 500 years ago and one of the oldest in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a photo from a guidebook published in the late 1980s, just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was it a building that enjoyed legal protection?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what we're looking amount now on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the same site, being used once again as a rubbish dump and as a deposit for junk cars. According to the Imam of the mosque who guided us to the site, the mosque was destroyed by JNA, Yugoslav National Army reservists, in the spring of 1992, the rubble removed by truck to a site called Ponor, 2 kilometres outside of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at another photograph of Nevesinje. Can you describe what's depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the Roman Catholic parish church in Nevesinje, a photo taken before the war, also a building that enjoyed legal protection. It was built in the Austro-Hungarian era at the beginning of the twentieth century, a very handsome building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What is depicted now in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the same site from the identical point of view. You can tell that the building is completely gone. I spoke with the parish priest, who now lives in Mostar. He described how the building had been bulldozed -- destroyed with explosives, the site bulldozed, and rubble also removed to the site mentioned previously, Ponor, 2 miles -- 2 kilometres outside of Nevesinje. Since the war, the local authorities, disregarding protests from the Catholic church, have not only refused to return control of the site and the adjacent parish house but are building a road through the site. According to the parish priest, ten years later not a single Catholic family has been able to return to Nevesinje or to reclaim its property there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the priest present in Nevesinje at the time that the church was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No. He was expelled before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to ascertain whether there was fighting during the time that the -- the church was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Nevesinje, like a number of other municipalities, had been taken over by the Serb nationalists before the outbreak of the war. There was no fighting in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Can you describe the photograph that we're looking at here on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the centre of Bosanska Krupa, a small town in North-western Bosnia. Like many towns in Bosnia, the town centre had the houses of worship of the three principal religious communities right facing each other in the centre. This is a photograph taken after the war. Unfortunately, I don't have a pre-war photo. But just to identify what you're looking at, on the right is the steeple of the Serbian Orthodox church; in the foreground at level are the ruins of the Roman Catholic church; and in the back is the minaret of the town's mosque, which was destroyed during the war and had just been reconstructed. If the photo quality were slightly better, you could see that the cupola on the top of the minaret is brand new.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the minaret that we're look at is --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Post-war reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could look at the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a pre-war photo of the Catholic church. You can compare it with the post-war photo and you can see the extent of the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in this particular photograph, we -- of the Catholic church, we are unable to see the minaret. Is that because of the angle of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. You're looking at it from further to the left and much closer to the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to the photograph on the right-hand side of the screen. Can you describe what's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is a photo of the mosque as it appeared right after the war, the minaret blown up, the mosque itself burnt out. This also was a monument under legal protection. It was built under Austro-Hungarian rule and was remarkable as an eclectic building with a Gothic rose window.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, these three houses of worship were in very close proximity to each other. Were you able to compare the damage done to the three buildings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian Orthodox church was completely intact. Both the Roman Catholic church and the mosque had been very badly damaged. The town was under the control of Bosnian Serb forces from the beginning of the war until the last weeks of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you now to look at some photographs from Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. What you're looking at is a photograph taken in the last year of the war, showing the rubble of the Catholic church, Catholic parish church in the centre of Prijedor in Northern Bosnia. You can see that the building has been demolished by some sort of blast, shattered timbers, remains of walls sticking out. Please note the modern building on the left, which is the parish centre, which you can also see in the pre-war photo. Yes, you can see that. The steeple was a very modern structure added not long before the war, but the church itself was quite old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the photograph that we see on the left-hand side of the screen is the pre-war photo.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the one on the right is as you found the site during your study.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, by the time I went, the site had been completely cleared of rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can draw your attention to the municipality of Bosanski Samac. What is depicted in the photograph we are now looking at on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: What we're looking at is a model and a photograph of the Catholic church in Bosanski Samac. It's a small town in North Central Bosnia. The person holding the photograph is the Catholic parish priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next photo, please. And what are we looking at now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the empty site of the parish church in Bosanski Samac. You can tell by the date-stamp that the photo was taken in October of 1996 by ICTY investigators. The church was behind the fence, which you see at the centre of the picture. In the background, you can see the Serbian Orthodox church of Bosanski Samac right across the street, completely undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain when the Catholic church was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to the priest who was in Bosanski Samac at the beginning of the war. He was forced to leave in -- early in the war in 1992, but a number of his parishioners were still in town when the church was destroyed in the beginning of 1993. They told him that the demolition Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the church was carried out with explosives but took a period of nearly two months because they didn't want to chance damaging the Orthodox church across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now draw your attention to the municipality of Srebrenica. If you could ask you to describe what we're looking at at the left-hand side of the screen. What's in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What you see on the left-hand side of the screen is a photograph of the Carsiska Dzamija, the Market mosque in Srebrenica. The photo was taken in the spring of 1995. It appears in the Dutch report on Srebrenica. The right-hand photograph was taken in January of 1996 by an Associated Press photographer. You can identify what you're looking at by looking at the tall street light, which you can also see next to the minaret in the left-hand photo. The mosque has been blown up. The minaret is gone. But because it was a modern reinforced concrete structure, the roof just pancaked down to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the dome that we see in the right-hand photograph is the same dome that we can see in the left-hand, pre-war photo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, but lower to ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you aware of what happened, what damage was done to the Serbian Orthodox church in Srebrenica during the time that it was held by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Serbian Orthodox church still stands, as far as I'm aware. The top of the steeple was damaged by shelling during the siege, but otherwise the church was intact. And in fact, I have seen Bosnian Serb videos showing General Mladic going to the church after his troops took Srebrenica, so we know it was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to the municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a drawing of the town mosque in Bratunac as it was on the eve of the war. Unfortunately, I was unable to find a photograph of the mosque before the war. The drawing was done by an exiled former resident of Bratunac and posted on a hometown website put up by homesick exiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'd ask you to take a look at the next photograph. What is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the site of the town mosque in Bratunac, with the usual deposits of rubbish. I could identify that it was a mosque by tracing foundations in the grass. Also, to the right of the picture there were some broken Muslim gravestones from the old graveyard next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now draw your attention to the next photograph. Can you tell us what's depicted in this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the cover of an Islamic religious monthly from the late 1980s. It shows the mosque in the village of Konjevic Polje, which is in Bratunac municipality, as it looked a few years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a photo I took of the same site. The gentleman is walking along the foundations of the mosque, which was completely destroyed in the spring of 1993, according to local eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can ask you to look at some photographs from the municipality of Banja Luka. Do you recognise what's in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Ferhadija Dzamija in Banja Luka, a 16th century mosque which was at one point nominated as a UNESCO protected site, a photograph from an architecture book from before the war. You can see to the left of the mosque a building in the background which you'll see in subsequent photographs. That is a 19th century building which houses the offices of the Islamic community. Next photo, please. This is a photo taken the -- in the days right after the mosque was destroyed in May of 1993. In the back you can see the same building. The mosque is gone. And here is a photo of the site as it looked after the war. You can see the bare outlines of the foundations of the mosque and the buildings of the muftistvo of the Islamic community offices in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your study, were you able to ascertain the circumstances surrounding the destruction of this mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I interviewed a number of people who were present in Banja Luka at the time, including the president of the Council of the Islamic Community at the time. And according to accounts, the area surrounding the mosque had been cordoned off by Bosnian Serb army troops on the evening before. After midnight there was a tremendous blast. The mosque was largely destroyed, as you saw on the photo. Then despite protests by the local Islamic community, the municipality of Banja Luka ordered out work crews, who with blasting and air hammers destroyed all that was left and moved all the rubbish, all the rubble to a rubbish dump outside of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to the final few locations that I will ask you to summarise in your testimony today, to the municipality of Visegrad. Can you describe what we're looking at in the photograph before us.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the old mosque, or Gazam Dzamija, in the centre of Visegrad, a photograph taken before the war which I obtained from the Institute of Protection of Monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the same site. I took the photo myself last summer. And I won't trouble you with it now, but close examination of pre-war and post-war photographs identifies all the buildings in the background as being the same ones. Otherwise, you could hardly tell, because it's gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you during every site -- or at every site that you visited, did you attempt to match locations that you could see in -- or buildings that you could see in pre-war photographs? Did you attempt to identify those buildings and orient your picture from the same angle that the original photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Insofar as possible. Also, in addition to pre-war photographs, I often had available extracts from cadastral registers with site plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony, you referred to being aware of reports coming out contemporaneous with the destruction of mosques. Was Visegrad one of the places where you were receiving reports about the destruction?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please summarise the reports that were coming out about Visegrad at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This was in August of 1992. Maggie O'Kane, a British reporter, visited Visegrad along with a colleague. They both filed stories reporting what they had seen, namely disturbed earth and mounds of rubble on the sites of two mosques in the centre Visegrad. They also reported interviewing refugees from Visegrad huddled outside the city limits who told them, "They destroyed the two mosques in the centre of Visegrad so we would not come back."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can now move to Sarajevo. Could I ask you to describe the picture that we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a photograph taken of the interior of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Sarajevo. At the bottom of the picture, you see charred books and manuscripts. More than 5.000 manuscripts were destroyed along with the archives. You can see the roof is open to the sky and the building has been burned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And photographs of -- the next photograph, can you describe what we're seeing?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is the building as it looked after the war. I looked very closely at the buildings surrounding it and none of them had -- showed any significant war damage. Very clearly, this building had been singled out. The institute occupied the top two floors of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what type of neighbourhood this building is situated in. What surrounds this building?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is in Sarajevo-Centar, the old centre of Sarajevo. It's very densely built. In front of the building is the main street, Marsal Tito Street, and then narrow side streets on the other three sides. It's nineteenth century office and apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a pre-war photo of a reading room in the National Library of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, a photo from a picture book published in the 1980s. And this is the burnt-out interior of the National Library, a photo taken in 1994 by a French photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, were there videos or video footage -- was there video footage taken of the destruction of the National Library in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I'm going to ask that the witness be shown three short clips - they're just a few seconds each - but it will take a matter of seconds to -- to load up each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to describe, Mr. Riedlmayer, what we're seeing in the photographs as the video plays.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: What you're seeing is the National Library on fire. This is the day after the shelling. This is the interior of the National Library. You can see the blaze is intense. You can see pages of books dancing in the flames and bookshelves in the background, skeletal. And so it's very consonant with the accounts by eyewitnesses, of whom either I or associates interviewed nearly a dozen, who describe exactly how the building was first targeted with -- with multiple -- with shells from multiple directions, that it was intense fire, that a lot of books went up in flames, that the firemen were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at the next clip. And after it's completed, if I could ask you to describe what we've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what we've seen in that clip?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: These are interviews with Sarajevo firemen, intercut with contemporary footage of the firemen fighting the fire. And what they describe is the difficulties they faced. I interviewed several of these firemen and they described how when they arrived on the scene they were targeted with heavy machine-gun fire and with anti-aircraft weapons pointed at street level, which cut up the hoses and injured a number of the firemen. Because of the cutoff of water, they had to go to the exposed banks of the Miljacka River right in front of the library to try to pump water but it was all in vain because the library eventually burnt out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did they report that the water to this part of the city had been disrupted?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This was earlier in the day. The shelling of the library started after sunset.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at the final clip and comment afterwards.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is -- the gentleman you saw at the very end with glasses and a goatee was the late Kurt Schork, a Reuter's correspondent who filed a detailed report on the burning of the library, which I've included as an annex to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was that the library that we were looking at in flames?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. This is television footage from that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last exhibit that the Prosecution will work with, or ask Mr. Riedlmayer to describe, is Prosecution Exhibit 488, tab 4. It's a map. The Chamber has copies of the map in the materials that have been provided. If we could just take a moment to put up a large version of the map, up on the easel, so Mr. Riedlmayer can describe what's depicted in the map. If it could just be rested on those clips. With the Court's permission, could Mr. Riedlmayer stand up and point to different portions of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, if you could stand to that side of the map. Could I ask you to describe generally what this map depicts.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here's Sarajevo. This is the Drina River. This is the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, could I ask you just to do it a little bit slower so we can all follow along.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you once again show us the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. The Drina River goes from the south -- the Drina River goes from the south - here's Foca, and here's Zvornik - and up to the north. The Sava River, which is the border with Croatia, goes this way. The Dalmatian coast is down there. The large green dots are major urban centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you indicate where some of the major cities are? Can you tell us where Sarajevo is?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sarajevo is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there are different coloured dots on this map that may not be visible on the television, but the Judges do have a copy of this map. Can you describe what the different coloured dots indicate.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The map attempts to plot the damaged, destroyed, and intact mosques in Bosnia as of the end of the war. Green dots, which are particularly dense in this north-west area, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be the Bihac region?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Bihac region -- represent intact mosques. Yellow dots, which you can see quite a lot around here in the area just south of Doboj, which was along the confrontation lines, represent damaged mosques. And red dots, which you can see pretty much everywhere, are destroyed mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you indicate for the Chamber where is the boundary line of the Republic of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: You can largely draw it by drawing a line between the red dots and all the others. The boundary pretty much goes -- if you start at Sarajevo, it goes like this, and then jogs south, and then roughly like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the Republic of Srpska, the territory of Republic of Srpska, is outlined by the presence of these red dots indicating destroyed mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, largely. The present-day Republika Srpska is somewhat smaller than the area eventually controlled during the war by Bosnian Serb forces, so some of the red dots spill over.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate for us the number of red dots indicating destroyed mosques that are contained on this map?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The number of red dots here is close to 900.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you yourself did not make this map.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did not make this map. The map was made by Mr. Bekir Besic, who is a refugee from Banja Luka currently living in Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the 900 locations indicated on this map by a red dot, how many of them did you personally visit during the course of your study?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I visited, I believe, close to 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The red dots represent what percentage of the total population of mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The red dots represent -- well, first of all, in the area occupied by Bosnian Serb forces, virtually every mosque was either heavily damaged or destroyed, more than 90 per cent. In terms of the total number of mosques in Bosnia, it's more than three-quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that the green -- the green dots, which represent those that were not damaged, that's a very small percentage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a small percentage, and it is concentrated in areas that remained under control of the Sarajevo government during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of your study, were you able to identify sites of destroyed mosques that you were able to ascertain resulted from direct involvement of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please give us some examples.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. For example, in the area around Doboj, which is right here, there were a number of sites where I interviewed eyewitnesses who described how Yugoslav forces, in the first week of May, had a direct hand in the destruction of mosques, in a place called Orasje, just on a hilltop south of Doboj. They described how a Yugoslav army transporter had come up the hill on Djurdjevdan, the feast of St. George, a Serb holiday, how the soldiers had strung explosives inside the mosque, how the men operating the plunger had taken the Imam ceremonial hat with the turban and put it on his head as he blew up the minaret, and how they had driven down the hill in the mostly Muslim neighbourhood, still wearing the same hat, and singing anti-Muslim songs. In other places, eyewitnesses described how mosques, and in one case a Catholic church, up near Brcko had been rocketed by Yugoslav army -- Yugoslav air force aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can I ask you to -- you've talked about a number of uses that the sites had been put to during the course of your summary. Can I ask you to indicate some of the locations and once again -- or summarise for us the types of uses that these sites were put to after the mosques were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Down in Foca, which is this town over here, the sites of former mosques in several instances were used as garbage dumps and places where garbage was being burned, also as parking lots for busses and as junk yards for abandoned cars. Your Honours have seen the site at Kozluk, where this big open space in the centre of town where the mosque had been was used for dumping rubbish. Similarly in Banja Luka, sites of mosques were used for dumping rubbish and the ruins were scrawled with anti-Muslim graffiti.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Groome. You told us earlier about a human rights council ordering compensation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- in respect of the destruction of one mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there any decision taken at a more general level as to whether mosques should be rebuilt or whether compensation should be paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were a number of cases between the -- before the Human Rights Chamber of Bosnia-Herzegovina, brought by the Islamic community in an effort to -- for secure control of the sites of the destroyed mosque, to secure permission for rebuilding. One of the cases involved 15 mosques in Banja Luka that had been destroyed, five mosques in Bijeljina, and the mosques in Janja. The case was brought in part because Bosnian Serb authorities used the permits process in order to prevent any rebuilding from taking place. A number of rulings on the admissibility and the merits were issued by the Human Rights Chamber, and I've appended them to my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But no, there hasn't been a case on a global level addressing all of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In conclusion, I'd ask -- or like to draw your attention to the case of Sacred Heart church in Doboj. And my question is: Are you aware of at least one instance where local Serbs attempted to mitigate the destruction of cultural property and records of their neighbours who were of different faiths?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please describe what you know about that situation.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This happened in Doboj. I had an interview with Don Pero Brkic, who is the Roman Catholic parish priest in Doboj. He described how on -- at the beginning of May of 1992 the Roman Catholic parish church in Doboj was destroyed. And in August of 1992, three Red Berets, wearing military uniforms, broke into the parish house and demanded of the parish priest - actually his aged predecessor, who has died since the war - that he turn over the parish records. However, the parish records had been hidden at the request of the priest by local people, Serbs, and -- at the beginning of May when the first attack on the church took place. These local good Serbs, as the priest referred to them, returned the records to the parish after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no more -- further questions. You may resume your seat, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I was wondering whether Mr. Riedlmayer or whether anybody else had made an estimate in monetary terms of the damage to the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I may ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, are you aware of any studies that have been done that would estimate, as Judge Robinson has enquired, the monetary loss of all this? Or can it be measured in terms of money?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, the problem with estimating monetary loss, of course, is you can easily estimate reconstruction costs, but in the case of things of great historic or artistic value, there's no way to compensate for the loss. I know that there have been figures mentioned in the press of various amounts. I don't know of any study that has been really systematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, before I move on to my concrete questions which have to do with your report and testimony, could you please tell me whether you know whether during those wars in Bosnia and Croatia -- because you're dealing with the period ranging from 1992 to 1995, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I thought so. Now, during those wars, were any religious sites or cultural monuments of Muslims or Croats on the territory of the Republic of Serbia either destroyed or damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have not carried out any studies in Serbia, obviously. I have read some reports, first of all, of a number of attacks on the Bajrakli Dzamija in Belgrade in which explosives were set, grenades thrown over the wall. Fortunately, neither injuries nor heavy damage resulted. However, there were attacks on some mosques in villages in the Sandzak, I understand. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask you whether there were any attacks. There are always extremists who can launch an attack of some kind or other. What I asked you was whether any of the facilities were destroyed at all. And I'm asking you that because the authorities, the police force, protected those monuments, because they knew of the existence of extremism which could cause damage. And when you mentioned Bajrakli Dzamija in Belgrade, that is a case in point. So I'm asking you: Was a single facility destroyed during all that time in Serbia, any facility at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't know of any that were destroyed in the same way that these mosques in Bosnia were, but I'm not basing this on personal knowledge; I have not been to Serbia since the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know -- I'm not asking you about the ways. I'm asking you whether -- do you know that a single mosque or facility, religious site, was destroyed in any way? Do you have knowledge of that at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I've told you what I know. That's about the limit of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Riedlmayer. Well, that is why I'm wondering what this report of yours has to do with Serbia at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's never been suggested it has to do with Serbia. It is a destruction -- a history, a report on destruction of community, cultural, and religious sites in Bosnia. It's always been that. Now, whether that has any connection with Serbia may be a matter which we will have to determine. It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Riedlmayer. Now, towards the end, just so that I don't forget, you mentioned that the JNA -- you described -- you made an astonishing statement that the JNA had destroyed some religious site in Orasje, I believe. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get that piece of information from?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I can tell you. I interviewed a resident of the village of Orasje - this is not the town of Orasje but a village near Doboj - who watched from his house which faces the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So somebody told you that over there. And when you say "Orasje," I was wondering how that was possible, because the -- it was the Croatian forces who had control of Orasje throughout the war, never the Serb forces. Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, the report that you compiled for the purposes of Mr. Groome is called "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1992-1996."

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that the contents should correspond to the title, the heading. So we're dealing here with the destruction of the cultural heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1992 to 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right. I would like to, however, correct something you said in your previous question, where you claimed that Orasje was under control of Croat forces. There's a town named Orasje in Northern Bosnia which was under the control of Croat militia. This is a village called Orasje in Doboj. It was not under Croat control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Riedlmayer. Well, all of that geography, I don't think we'll ever be able to learn the entire geography of it all. But tell me this, please: Do you distinguish between cultural and religious heritage, or rather, monuments of cultural and religious monuments?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The two are obviously interrelated in any situation. The reason I phrased it in this way is because there are cultural heritage sites that have no direct connection with religion, like, say, the historical archives and the National Library. Also, there are religious sites which are very recent. Obviously they're manifestations of culture, but they're not cultural heritage in the same way as an ancient site. It's semantics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, doubtless a link does exist, but as you said, they were two specific things. You said that there was a connection, a direct -- a connection between those two things. Now, is it true - not to lose time - that the international conventions insist upon the protection of cultural monuments as the common heritage of mankind? So the protection of cultural monuments is what they refer to, generally speaking; is that right? Of course, the protection of religious sites is also necessary - and I don't bring that into question at all - but I'm saying that international covenants and conventions refer to the protection of cultural monuments.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm not appearing as a legal expert. However, I would like to point out that, in addition to The Hague Convention, which does speak of the cultural heritage of mankind, there are also a number of other international legal conventions that specifically address the protection of religious monuments as well, ranging from the Geneva Conventions on land and sea warfare to the Geneva Conventions enacted after World War II and their protocols additional. The language of some of these is much more inclusive than what you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, of course nobody reasonable questions the need for the protection of religious sites. I'm asking you this because your report is entitled "The Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's the term you use. And you wrote it to lend greater importance to it, and in your opinion this means that religious monuments represent cultural heritage, which is untenable from the professional aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know what the question means. What's the -- what is the point? Are you saying that the religious monuments are being downgraded in the report or something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. May. What I'm saying is that the title, "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina," that is the wording of it, so I'm asking the expert whether that means that religious monuments are without exception cultural monuments, cultural heritage in conformity with international conventions.
