I'm not bringing into question the need to protect religious sites and monuments at all. I'm just saying that greater importance is being lent here to what is being explained. So we're not only dealing with cultural monuments here in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, if you can comment on that, by all means do, and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. All I can comment is, first of all, in my report I specified which of these monuments were under legal protection and, therefore, presumably of great cultural or historical importance. I also had a breakdown by the age of the building. So I think if you get past the title and look at the substance of the report, it should be quite clear what is what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Riedlmayer, you'll remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. And that includes the Prosecution team. If the legal officer would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I address you in private session on an administrative matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'll withdraw and Mr. Agha will be here for the Prosecution on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have up to one hour and a quarter, if you require it, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I only had under ten minutes before the break, as you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, from your report, I see that you covered only 19 municipalities out of all the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were your criteria on the basis of which you selected those particular municipalities? Because this is, after all, less than half all the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I was given an initial list of municipalities that were of particular interest, and I was given free choice for others to select. I selected additional ones on the basis of a variety of factors, including trying to assure some geographic spread and looking at areas of different ethnic composition. I clearly, within the time available to me, did not have time to cover all of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't have any particular criterion on the basis of which you selected those 19 municipalities. Those were assigned to you, in a sense, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The ones of particular interest, yes. Presumably there are the ones where, you know, full proof is being sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. Tell me, please: With respect to those 19 municipalities at least, did you make an accurate list of monuments of cultural heritage in those 19 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't understand the question. What do you mean "an accurate list"? I tried to be very accurate in my description of each site visited and I tried to include every site of important -- I describe in my report the very sources I had, amongst which were listings of sites by the Institute for Protection of Monuments, by the various religious authorities and others, so yes, I tried to have as accurate a compilation as possible before I went.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I can't quite fully understand your whole answer. So let me clarify my question. If you did have a complete list of all monuments of cultural heritage, covering all monuments of cultural heritage, not just religious structures, did you compare that list of all the monuments of cultural heritage with the list of damaged or destroyed religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again, I don't quite understand what you mean. Yes, I -- I had the list of registered cultural monuments. A subset of those were religious structures, and religious structures seemed to have suffered disproportionate damage, which is why they figured to such a large extent in the study. Also consider that in Bosnia-Herzegovina cultural and ethnic identity historically has been tied up with the religious choices of one's ancestors and that, therefore, a religious monument tends to have an association with a particular cultural and ethnic group, which is presumably also why they figured to such a large degree in the destruction and this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is the ratio between the total number of monuments of cultural heritage and religious structures that were damaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The total number of monuments of cultural heritage includes a very large number of sites of a sort that I didn't include in this study. For example, medieval cemeteries, ruined castles, and so forth. For the most part, these didn't suffer damage in the war; in any case I don't have a calculation of, you know, what the percentages are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you think it would be important to establish the overall situation with all monuments of cultural heritage and the percentage of religious structures destroyed? Because obviously these two categories are not one and the same. They can be, but they need not be in the same category.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, I based my judgement in part on surveys done after the war by the Council of Europe, by the Institute for Protection of Monuments, which, as you suggest, did cover monuments other than religious monuments in a much more comprehensive manner. And the fact is that most of these other categories of cultural monuments did not suffer to the same degree that religious monuments did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the crux of the issue that I addressed at the beginning, because in your report entitled "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia and Herzegovina," whereas now you yourself say that most of the monuments of cultural heritage are not religious structures or, rather, that it was the religious structures that were destroyed most. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Certainly the religious structures were the ones that were destroyed to the greatest degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, since you didn't quite understand why I was asking this question, and now from the explanation of Mr. Riedlmayer we see that what is called cultural heritage or monuments of cultural heritage is a much broader category, I consider this matter important because you as a lawyer certainly know that reciprocal destruction of religious structures is the religious component of a civil war, whereas destruction of monuments of culture would be tantamount to genocide. That is why in Mr. Riedlmayer's report we see that it deals with the destruction of religious monuments as the religious component of the civil war that was being waged there, rather than the latter, that is, destruction of monuments of culture. And that is why I made my remarks and asked questions relevant to the title of this report, which is "Destruction of cultural heritage." And of course, they did, all three sides, destroyed each other's monuments in this civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on, Mr. Riedlmayer. Is it true that the cultural heritage of Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of monuments of culture of all three ethnicities living in the area and who lived there for centuries together? Therefore, it includes the monuments of the Serb people as well, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, your report is limited only to Roman Catholic and Islamic religious structures. Why? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I made that clear in the direct examination. These were the terms of reference of the study I was asked to undertake. And therefore, I limited myself to that. I would like to point out, however, that in my writings, some of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which are appended to the report, I have dealt with the issue of destruction of Serbian Orthodox monuments in Bosnia-Herzegovina that -- I would also like to say that I did observe during my survey the state of Serbian Orthodox monuments. I did observe some destruction, especially in village areas in Herzegovina and in North-Western Bosnia. However, the fact is that in all major centres that I have visited that remained under the control of Bosnian government forces during war, the Serbian Orthodox monuments have survived; whereas, the same cannot be said of the population centres under the control of Bosnian Serb forces. So I think it's wrong to assume that there was some sort of equality of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. You say that Serbian Orthodox monuments have survived. I have a book here regarding the extermination of Serbs. It covers 1992 and 1993. I don't have 1995. And if it is of any interest to you, please have a look at it. It is provided also in the Serbian language, in Cyrillic, and also in the English language, "Destruction of Orthodox Religious Structures," and quite a long list is contained in the book of those monuments. So please have a look from the page I have opened the book on. And you can place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's let the witness have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the book. I'm also familiar with the structure on the ELMO. It's the Serbian Orthodox church in Trnovo, which is a village on the road from Sarajevo to the Drina Valley in the east. I also have photographs of my own taken in 1996 of the same church. I passed through Trnovo last summer, and the church is now repaired. It is one of roughly 20 such structures which are illustrated in this book. As I say, I don't have any animus against describing and condemning such destruction. All I'm saying is that was not in the terms of my mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you go on, can you tell us, please, the title of the book, who it's by, something of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The book is called "Iskorenjivanje Srba u Bosnia-Herzegovine," "The Eradication of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." It was published in 1994 by Rad. And the authors are Drago Jovanovic, Gordana Bundalo and Milos Govedarevic. I think it was originally published by -- with support by Canadian Serb Immigration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps it might be helpful. You say you saw about -- or you know of 20 such sites of Orthodox churches which were damaged or destroyed. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm saying there are about 20 that are illustrated in this book. The book is about much more than just cultural destruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That we can see. Well, Mr. Milosevic, do you want the witness to look at any more photographs in the book?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let him leaf through the book further on from the page that we opened the book to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The page he was at. And just perhaps you would confirm that there are about 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not 20. There's a list containing many more. I'm not talking about 20. The witness mentioned 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is -- I'm sorry. What I'm saying is there are more listed, however, there are only 20 which are photographs. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then perhaps you could give us some idea of how many there are listed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The -- the list is -- includes 68 items. Now, some of them are sites which I visited and I know from having visited them that the damage description is not correct. I wouldn't doubt that, however, as a range of magnitude that represents a good approximate count of how many were damaged or destroyed in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just turn over a few more pages to show those photographs on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Sure. This is Trnovo again, the same one you saw at the beginning. This is in Northern Bosnia, Luzine, some cemetery chapels in Posavina. This is in Derventa. This is another cemetery chapel near Brod. And this is the parish church in Bosanski Brod. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as you can see, have you any reason to think that those are not accurate photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the photographs I have no doubt are accurate. What I'm saying is the verbal descriptions in some cases, especially of sites for which there are no photographs, are inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In case we need it, for future reference, can you give us the pages on which those photographs appear, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The section begins with page 205 and runs through 220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want to ask any more questions about the book, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I would like to tender those photographs into evidence, if possible. They could be photocopied, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course the list attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit the photographs subject to the -- if somebody has them photographed -- photocopied for us, pages 205 to 220. This will be subject to any objection which the Prosecution may make in due course if they have reason to object. So can we do that, please, and give it the next Defence number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I'll ask the registry to photocopy the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the book in front of me now, Mr. Riedlmayer, but you said there were about 68 sites listed, is that right, in the book?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you are aware of the fact that this is for 1993 -- 1992 and 1993, so this is only a partial report. It doesn't cover the whole period. The war went on for another two years. And even then, they didn't have all the data they needed for those two years. So do you have any idea of the number of cultural sites and religious structures of Serbs destroyed in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I indicated to you, I did not make a systematic survey. However, I'm aware that there were Serbian churches that were destroyed in the last year of the war. I saw some of them, in villages, for example, near Sanski Most. The number was not very large, but the churches had definitely been burned out. But I would hazard a guess that the total number would not have more than doubled at the very most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will have occasion to present evidence about that. But for instance, in that book, under number 1, an old monastery is listed, Zitomislic. Due to chance, it comes as number 1 in that book. You will remember that you wrote - and I have this noted down - "On the History, Significance, and Destruction of the Zitomislici Monastery Complex" by Andras Riedlmayer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I did write a short article about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to recall, for example -- you say the following: "In July 1992, an expedition of the [In English] Croatian Defence union set out from the town of -- from town of Medjugorje, the popular pilgrimage site for visions of the Virgin Mary"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I recall the quotation you're reading. It, however, is not from the section of that website that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Are they your words? You say, "The force was allegedly accompanied by Dr. Vlado --"

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I say, that is -- that is not my section of that article. That part of the article was written by someone else. The history, significance, et cetera, is lower down on the same website. But just not to get lost in details, I can tell you I don't contest the fact that the monastery at Zitomislic was destroyed by HVO, the Croat nationalist militia, in 1992. And I've written about it not only on that website but in a number of other articles, some of which have been submitted as annexes to my report. It is perhaps the single most significant Serbian Orthodox site in Bosnia to have been destroyed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And are these your words -- or rather, is this correct, that "The HVO attacked the ancient Serbian monastery of Zitomislic, killing the monks, and systematically annihilating this ancient and priceless sacral site. [In English] As this text is being written, the HVO refuses to allow public access to the remains of the Zitomislic monastery complex"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again, I don't disagree with the text but that part is not my part of it. I didn't write that part. I wrote the historical section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have here on the history, significance, and destruction of Zitomislic by Andras Riedlmayer - it's been highlighted - but you don't question that what I read out is correct; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to place this on the ELMO, but I'd like to have it exhibited, just this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see what it is, first of all. If you show it to the witness, first, to identify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, the section you highlighted is authored by Michael Sells. At the bottom of the page is the header for my part, which is on the following page. So it's not my words, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. What it is is Michael Sells, who's a professor at Haverford College in the United States, has set up a website dedicated to various cultural sites in Bosnia that were destroyed during the war. One of his pages is devoted to Zitomislic, and I helped provide photographs and a short historical abstract for the site. What Mr. Milosevic was reading aloud is part of Michael Sells' introduction. The section on the history follows, and it's not on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nonetheless, we'll -- we'll exhibit the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, so you do have, if not the complete -- a complete knowledge, at least partial knowledge about the destruction of religious structures belonging to the Serb people. And as I can see, you wrote something about the subject too. But you didn't include any of that in this report of yours. How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think I have explained it. It was not part of the terms of my mission that I was asked to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Quite clear, I think. Mr. Groome, or rather his side over there, asked you exclusively for the Muslim and Catholic religious structures that were damaged or destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The terms of the mission were to look at the religious and cultural heritage of the non-Serb communities, in effect, in the municipalities studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the non-Serb communities," that means that your mandate was to exclude the damage done on Serb religious structures and sites and cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with this. He's explained the position. He's here to give evidence about those subjects, which he has done. Now, it doesn't seem to me we can take it any further. No, he didn't give evidence and he hasn't given evidence about the Serb -- destruction on the Serb side. He wasn't asked to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Mr. Riedlmayer is testifying precisely to the fact that his mandate or term of reference was to exclude the Serb structures, religious structures, and cultural structures which were damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Because they cannot be relevant to the charges which we're dealing with in this trial. That is why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine, Mr. May. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, your research, Mr. Riedlmayer, does it indicate precisely the fact that during the war in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina that what happened was a mutual destruction of religious sites of the two warring sides, of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your overall research, does it indicate that during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there was a mutual destruction of religious sites by the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The answer to that is that yes, there were some elements of tit-for-tat destruction. However, this did not all happen to equal degrees, nor did it happen simultaneously. And as I explained, in the areas that were under the control of Bosnian Serb forces during the war, there seems to have been a nearly complete eradication of non-Serb religious structures, whether Catholic churches or Muslim mosques. In the areas under control of the Sarajevo government forces, especially in the urban centres, by and large Serbian Orthodox sites survived intact. The places where there were attacks on Serbian Orthodox sites tended to be in rural areas and most often at the end of the war. In addition, in the early phases of the war, in Herzegovina especially, to some degree in the Posavina region of Northern Bosnia, Croat militias acting outside the control of the Sarajevo government staged attacks on Serbian Orthodox sites. I have seen and I indeed documented some of these, but not for the purposes of this study.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Riedlmayer. I see that in your report, as you selectively limited your research just to 19 municipalities. I see you haven't gone further than that. Now, as you're speaking about two sides, and during the war there were three sides, three parties to the conflict and war, do you have any knowledge in view of that, any data, or did you delve at all into the question of how far, for example, the Catholic churches were destroyed by the Muslim forces, for example? How many of them? Or how many Muslim religious sites were destroyed in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Croatian forces, for example? Did you consider issues of that kind and make an analysis on the basis of that kind of data?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was destruction of this sort during the 1993/1994 conflict between Croatian forces and Muslim forces; however, none of the 19 municipalities that I studied fell into the area where this fighting happened. As a result, I have no data or first-hand observations to make. I don't know if this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Yes, it does answer my question, in fact, that you're viewing it partially, just a part, which can be ascribed to the Serb side. Now, tell me this, please: For those 19 municipalities, before you undertook your research work, did you attempt to ascertain exactly which cultural monuments existed in each of those individual municipalities, before the war began?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I had listings of various sorts from publications from the republican level, heritage authorities, and also information from the Catholic Church and the Islamic community regarding the religious monuments that were not listed sites. So yes, I did have a pretty good notion of what was there before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you speak about religious structures. But as we noted the difference a moment ago between cultural structures and religious structures, that they don't always coincide. They need not always be one in the same thing, did you try and establish the ratio of cultural structures and religious structures for each of those municipalities, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think we've been through this. But if you look at my report, you can see that I carefully listed which of the particular monuments enjoyed legal protection and which did not. I also had a breakdown by age of monument, which doesn't always correspond. Not every old monument is necessarily listed for legal protection. I don't have a breakdown by municipality. But using my database, I could probably easily produce one. If you have a printout of my database, you probably saw that it has a field specifying whether a particular site was a listed monument, meaning under legal protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I hope we're not disputing the fact that the difference between cultural and religious heritage is of substantial -- of a substantial nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through this. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In point 2.1 of your report, and it is entitled "Damage to Islamic cultural heritage." "Damage to Islamic architectural heritage" is the title,"Damage to Islamic architectural heritage." You say that of the 277 mosques in 19 municipalities in which the research was conducted, 71 mosques were registered as cultural heritage, a cultural monument under the protection of the state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's right. Of the mosques surveyed, 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, does that mean that in this total mass of damaged Islamic religious sites that cultural monuments make up 26.3 per cent? And in view of the title of your research, it can refer to just a quarter of the structures that you deal with in your report, in your survey, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, if you refer cultural monument as a monument that has been singled out for legal protection, yes. If you refer to it in a broader sense, no. You will note also that of those mosques, 161 dated from the Ottoman or Austro-Hungarian era, and therefore were monuments of some antiquity and value, whether or not they had actually been singled out for legal protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But then is it correct that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there wasn't wide-scale, systematic destruction of cultural heritage -- but rather mutual, reciprocal, which of course is also without justification, can't be justified, but that it was the two -- the sides mutually destroying each other's religious and cultural structures? Is that right, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do not agree, respectfully. The -- first of all, the cultural heritage subsumes the religious monuments. And yes, there was a wide-scale and systematic destruction of these. And the systematic destruction was particularly severe in the areas controlled by Bosnian Serb forces and targeted the structures of the non-Serb communities. So yes, that is true. If you broaden the sample and include all listed sites, many of them are archaeological sites, there would be no particular reason or particularly easy means to target a -- an archaeological site. I believe that the question here is not just buildings but their connection with a particular group that has -- is alleged to have been singled out for persecution. And therefore, the sites have value beyond merely the -- their particular characteristics or antiquity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand your explanation, Mr. Riedlmayer. Is it true that the programme for Islamic architecture, the Aga Khan, at the Harvard University that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't catch the verb. Could the accused repeat what he said, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are asked by the interpreter to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'm asking you whether it's true that you are a bibliographer of the programme for Islamic architecture of the Aga Khan, attached to the Harvard University.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that within the frameworks of that programme you also dispose of a documentation centre. Who is financing that particular programme?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance -- it is relevant, Mr. May, because of the obvious bias and prejudice of an expert with respect to his professional orientation and his employment when it comes to Muslim religious structures, and the report itself demonstrates that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Riedlmayer, it's suggested you are biased in favour of Muslim religious structures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm biased against the destruction of any religious structures of any description. As far as my employment goes, I'm employed by Harvard University, but I am speaking here in my own capacity. The programme referred to is one of a number of endowed programmes at Harvard University. This was endowed by His Highness the Aga Khan, who was an old graduate of Harvard University and who 25 years ago gave a donation to Harvard University to establish a chair for the study of Islamic architecture, and as part of the support structure for that chair, a documentation centre was set up, which I've directed since 1985. That speaks to my specialisation as an art documentation professional, but it doesn't have any bearing on whether or not I can be impartial in the context of a study such as this. It merely speaks to my qualifications, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. I assume that any civilised person is opposed to the destruction of religious structures. That doesn't have to do -- need not have anything to do with any expert qualities or qualifications for cultural monuments as such. Now, you quoted an example that some, as you called them, good Serbs protected and defended the archives of a Catholic church, I believe, if I understood you correctly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. The term was that of the parish priest in Doboj, who said, "good people, local Serbs," who, at his request, hid the archives after the first attack on the Doboj Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I received information to the effect that the leadership of Republika Srpska, on many occasions, issued strict orders prohibiting the destruction or attacks on religious sites and structures. Do you have any information about that, any example along those lines?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have no information on that, but I must say that if -- if they had in fact done so, it seems to have been spectacularly ineffective, judging by the evidence on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all three sides were ineffective, as far as I can see. But here among the many that we're probably going to be able to find in due course, I have here a photocopy of an order by the president of the Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, which was sent to the different centres. This one in particular refers to -- it is sent to the Ministry of the Interior, to Minister Ratko Adzic in person. "On the basis of Article 80 of the constitution of Republika Srpska, I hereby order that through the security services centre of Banja Luka strengthened patrols be set up to secure all religious sites and protect them from repeated terrorist actions. The order should be carried out forthwith and measures taken and please inform me of the results." This can be placed on the overhead projector. So he qualifies this as being a terrorist attack, what took place in Banja Luka, and hereby issues this order, according to which the security centre should protect all religious sites, and this also referred to other municipalities as well. But we can't now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before it is exhibited, what language is it in, Mr. Milosevic? Is it in the original?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point putting it on the ELMO. We'll mark it for identification. Perhaps you could just look at it, Mr. Riedlmayer, just to -- Just a moment. Just confirm it says what the accused says it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a quick reading, it seems to say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it. Give it an exhibit number, mark it for identification only until it's translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as far as I know, Mr. Riedlmayer speaks Serbian. Isn't that right, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he's done that. Mark it for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D159 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm doing my best to speed this up, Mr. Riedlmayer, the cross-examination, I mean. You say in your report that a commission for the protection of national heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up pursuant to the Dayton Agreement, and it's annex number 8, in fact. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, however, is it true that the commission was set up under the auspices and along with the administrative support of UNESCO, in fact, and that in that sense it worked from 1996 to the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: It was set up with representation from UNESCO. It's a mixed body. Along with the Human Rights Chamber, it was one of two bodies specified in the Dayton Accord to have jurisdiction over all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And like the Human Rights Chamber, it had mixed international and local membership. Currently it operates under the supervision of the Bosnia-Herzegovina joint presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in its work - when I say "its," I mean the commission's work - from the beginning, that the Republican Institute for the Protection of Cultural and Historical Heritage of Republika Srpska took part, is that right, and that it sent historical technical photo documentation that it had to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I'm not privy to the deliberations of the commission, which has never published any records of its proceedings. However, I do know that there was a representative appointed from the Republika Srpska, as from the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on the basis of annex 8 of the Dayton Agreement, as the framework, and the exclusive jurisdiction of the commission was the fact that the decision be taken on the proclamation of movables or immovables, being national monuments in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Those were the terms of its reference, and the main task of the commission during the first years of its existence was to arrive at a list of so-called national monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that this particular republican institute for the protection of cultural monuments of Republika Srpska, the one I mentioned a moment ago, in elaborating a proposal for including in the list of national cultural monuments used methodology which implied that each proposal had to be attended by basic data about the property, such as location, historical data, evaluation, photo and technical documents wherever possible, and so on and so forth? So methodology that was prescribed, in fact, for this kind of work. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not really privy to the proceedings of the commission on national monuments, which did not deliberate in public and has not published any of its proceedings or terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are you saying? That the -- you didn't have access to the transcripts? Did you try to get them and somebody didn't give you access to them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The answer is affirmative. I tried to get them, and in fact they were not made public, so I wasn't able to access them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who refused to give them to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did not make a formal request. I made inquiries and was told that they were not public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that the work of the commission was interrupted at the point at which, according to my information, there were 777 monuments under investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I say, I'm not familiar with the work of the commission for the reasons specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you at least know who made up the commission, in addition to the two international representatives, as far as my information tells me, the representative of the Muslim side, a man named Rizman Begovic, and the Croatian side was represented by a man called Palameta, who was mentioned in connection with the destruction of Zitomislici and the text that we exhibited a moment ago, because he was an expert, and the representatives on the Serb side, Bradar and Rasul. Do you remember perhaps -- do you at least have any knowledge as to the members of the commission, two representatives from the international community, one from the Muslim side, one Croat and two Serbs? And I gave you the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I know that the -- that was the national breakdown of the commission. I don't recall the names, but I have no reason to doubt that the names you mentioned are probably the ones who did serve on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you saw in the text that you read out on the page on which the title of your paper figures also, "The historical significance of Zitomislic," that Vlado Palameta, an art historian from Stolac, became a member of that commission. Do you have any reason to doubt the facts listed over there that you read out, and also do you doubt that he was a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't doubt that he was a member of the commission. As far as his participation in the destruction of Zitomislici, I know that that was alleged at the time. He was known to be closely linked to Mate Boban and the ruling clique in the Croat nationalist para-state at the time, and it may well be that he was indeed responsible, but I have no proof of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you believe that someone who took part in razing to the ground a monastery of that kind, the church of which was built --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop. He can't comment on all this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that fact call in question the work and results of the work of that commission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, is anything in your report based on data collected by that commission?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No. As I told you, I had no access to the files of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have nothing as a source of your information that would be traced back to that commission.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that its commission stopped working when it had reached the figure of 777 monuments of cultural heritage, did that study cover a somewhat broader area than your own report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I assume that the commission was covering the whole territory of Bosnia and not just the 19 municipalities that were the subject of my study. And in addition, I assume that it was looking at a much broader range of sites, including archaeological sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. Tell me, please: Since on page 8, paragraph 4 of your report you say that a member of your research team was Professor Dr. Muhamed Hamidovic, dean of the faculty of architecture in Sarajevo, a former director of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural, Historical, and Natural Heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that he was replaced in his position as director of the institute?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. He's now dean of the faculty of architecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And is it true that the reason for his replacement was that he didn't allow conservation work in Zavala, in Popovo Polje, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Such an act -- let us assume that it is correct. Would you consider such an act to be a discriminatory one and not an objective attitude to take?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I say, I have no knowledge of why he may have disagreed with that project, if he indeed did so. He may have had professional reasons. I also know that the restoration work at Zavala is going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, it's not thanks to him. But tell me, please: Is it true that certain responsible international bodies, like, for instance, the committee for cultural heritage of the Council of Europe, compiled their reports containing data on damage done to cultural heritage of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The Council of Europe's survey, which resulted in a report called action plan, which is cited in my report here - let's see. Just a moment - okay, I have an annex on sources, and this is listed under A1.2, Council of Europe. And they did this study in collaboration with authorities in both entities in Bosnia in 1997/1998, and in March 1999 they published a report called "Specific action plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina, preliminary phase." They had as their original project the coverage of all listed monuments in Bosnia-Herzegovina of any description. For a variety of reasons, they were not able to achieve that goal in some municipalities due to difficulty of access and other issues. I describe the project, which I used as one of my sources, and both its merits and shortcomings. I stand on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have described the project as one of your sources, for the reasons that you have already explained did you leave out everything that belonged to the cultural heritage to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, we've been through this. We really have. And it's just wasting time. What's your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is it true that your report has a clearly discriminatory and selective approach to the topic. "Destruction of the Cultural Heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina" is its title, yet you are limiting yourself to only two ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you've asked him about bias, and he's given you an answer. And you've asked him a great deal about -- about destruction of Serb churches, and he's given you answers about those. Now, you've got about a quarter of an hour left, if that, so you'll need to use the time usefully, if you have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do have a sufficient number of questions that would even require a little more time. But as you say, I asked him a lot about Serb churches; I asked him very little about Serbian churches. I still plan to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is it true that you had direct insight or actually visited a little over half of the sites that you cover in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for more than 40 per cent of the sites, you used other sources; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which other sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I specify them in my report. I have a detailed annex, and, you know, if you want, I can read through them, but I don't see the benefit. What I can say is that I used no information that was not supported by photographs and, if possible, corroborated by second and even third independent means of verification, and that I limited myself to sources that I can considered to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Riedlmayer: Incomplete sites, can they be considered religious sites, and especially cultural heritage sites, if they haven't been finished?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, an uncompleted building is -- if it's a religious building, is a religious site. When you go to a place and you're looking for a church or a mosque, you include, you know, every structure of that sort that you might come across. So yes, an uncompleted one is a religious site. It's not an active religious site, and I make a point in my study in showing that inactive sites, meaning either a mosque or a church that had yet to be dedicated, or, for example, as in the case of the Cuckova Dzamija, a mosque in Nevesinje which had been disused since World War II, these particular structures tended to escape destruction, even in areas where every other religious structure had been damaged or destroyed. So yes, including these made sense for the purposes of the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether this -- I should like to leave aside for the moment that absolutely not a single word of justification can be found for the destruction of anybody's religious sites, but I'm asking you as a professional whether an incomplete structure can be considered a cultural site, regardless of the intention behind its construction.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: If you define cultural sites as monuments under protection, I don't know of any incomplete buildings that have been designated as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. Since you had in mind, even though that was not part of your assignment -- but you're an intellectual, a professional, you must have learnt about various circumstances and events, even though you didn't cover them, for the reasons that you have given and explained. You did not cover any Serbian religious structures or monuments of cultural heritage. Leaving that aside for the moment, my question is: Did you have in mind the chronology of destruction, any kind of chronology in the sequence of destruction?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Insofar as possible, obviously, first of all, I was visiting these sites after the war. So I could not determine just from looking at a site when it was destroyed. What I did try to do, insofar as possible, is to find informants, contemporary first-hand media reports, and other information which would indicate when the particular site had been damaged or destroyed. While I didn't do a statistical compilation for the purposes of the report, going through this study, which I've done countless times, I can come to some general conclusions, one of which is that the vast majority of the destruction of mosques and Catholic churches happened in the first year, year and a half of the war. In most places, it happened around the same time that there was the forcible expulsion of minority populations. In some cases, it happened after the people had been expelled. They report that the mosque or the church was still standing when they left; and when they came back after the war, it was gone. In terms of -- since you asked, in terms of the Serbian Orthodox churches, I can detect two phases that seemed to have taken place. In rather limited areas, namely in the Neretva Valley in Herzegovina in the south, and in the Posavina region in the north, where there was fighting between Bosnian Serb forces and Croat militias, there was a good deal of what you describe as the reciprocal attacks. Many of them seemed to have targeted cemetery chapels, which were close to the battlefronts in any case. Most spectacularly, in terms of really important monuments were places like Zitomislic or the Serbian cathedral in Mostar. However, there was no widespread attacks on Serbian churches in other parts of Bosnia. There were isolated instances, like the church in Trnovo that you showed. At the very end of the war, in the final weeks, especially in Western Bosnia, as the Serbian military front collapsed and Croat and Muslim forces surged forward, there was some burning of Serbian village churches in Western and North-Western Bosnia, and I saw a number of those. What is somewhat significant there is that this was not by any means universal and it did not seem to occur in the major urban centres. So in the centre of Kljuc, for example, the Catholic church and the town mosque had all been destroyed while the Serbs were in occupation. When the town was retaken by Croat and Muslim forces, the Serb church was left intact. Similarly in Bosanska Krupa, which we showed earlier on the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's in fact time to adjourn. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, you've got ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a little more, please, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider it. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have 15 minutes more, a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean a total of 25 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've given me five extra minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us cover a few more questions, Mr. Riedlmayer. I don't doubt that you consider the chronology of events to be of significance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, when you're talking about the destruction of the mosque in Grapska, that there was a Serbian Orthodox church in that same location and that the mosque was destroyed after the Serbian Orthodox church was gravely damaged? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: May I please check my database? The site in Grapska is one which I didn't visit personally, so I don't know what was in the surroundings. I only have photo documentation on the site. I don't have any information for you on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't have information about that, do you know that the Saborna Crkva [phoen] and the Metropol [phoen] in Mostar, the Zitomislic in Klepci, the church in Derventa, the Ascension church, et cetera, that these churches were destroyed by mining in June 1992, almost a year prior to the destruction or damage to mosques and Catholic churches in the area? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Mostar was not one of the municipalities in my survey. But as a matter of fact, I know that the destruction of mosques and Catholic churches in Mostar occurred prior to June 1992, during the April and early May siege of Mostar by the JNA. It has been extensively documented, and I have seen many photographs of destroyed heritage in Mostar. Almost all of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the mosques in Mostar and both Catholic churches in Mostar were destroyed in this siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my data, both in Mostar and Klepci and Derventa, et cetera, the churches were destroyed before the mosques or the Catholic churches were destroyed. But you have obviously different information. Is it clear -- is it clear that the revanchism under conditions of war which has a religious component to it is something that triggers the response of the other side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not for the witness to answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 15 of your report, you mention certain Roman Catholic churches which were either intact or lightly damaged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you mention there the Zupna church in Banja Luka, the Catholic churches in Rogatica, Trebinje, Pale, which were not damaged, but on the contrary, they were preserved by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do mention the Banja Luka church. Trebinje and Pale were not among the municipalities that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Rogatica was also not among the municipalities in this survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 10 of your report, in paragraph 1, you say that it is possible that those who were destroying mosques were acting on the basis of some sort of a list. Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I merely suggest that this is one conclusion one could draw from the fact that, number one, destruction of mosques in certain areas was quite thorough and yet incomplete mosques were left alone. The other reasons that led me to that conclusion are the following: One is that the destruction of mosques was often carried out with the use of explosives. I would assume that in wartime access to explosives and the knowledge to use them and the organisation required -- and manpower required would involve at the very least the acquiescence of the authorities in control of the area. Also, the destruction in many places, especially urban areas, took place while the area was under curfew. Again, it seems hard to believe that this would be a spontaneous activity on someone's part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. We have to save time. Do you believe that the other two sides that were destroying each other's churches - and I am talking about Muslim and Catholic and Serb Orthodox structures - also acted on the basis of some kind of list?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: As I have made clear, the reciprocal destruction of village churches and mosques in the Muslim-Croat conflict of 1993/1994 was not the focus of this study. I did not visit any of the municipalities where that kind of fighting took place, and I have no data to rely on. Whether or not people operated from lists, I don't know, but I can judge from the fact that it probably was not a widespread policy, by the fact that, for example, in Sarajevo or Tuzla or even Zenica the Catholic and Orthodox churches have survived, which is certainly not the case of Catholic churches and mosques in most towns in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But we also mentioned some towns and also some buildings that remained intact. You also mentioned some. I must say not comprehensively, but in passing only. Tell me, Mr. Riedlmayer, when preparing your report, did you try to establish how many mosques or churches or minarets or bell towers that were destroyed or damaged were used for military purposes precisely by those who were using them as their own religious temples?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Conducting the survey as I did, at some remove from the war events, obviously there were some limits to what I could establish along these lines. However, at each monument that I was able to visit or for which I had good photographic documentation, I would note several features. Whether or not there was any evidence that the building had suffered small arms fire impact, which usually is an indication that there was fighting in the area; also, I always took note of the context. If there were surrounding buildings, whether they had been damaged or not. Finally, it is indisputable - and I note it in my report - that in a number of towns where large numbers of mosques and Catholic churches were destroyed, for example, 15 mosques in Banja Luka and a couple in the suburbs or 5 mosques in Bijeljina, that these -- or in Nevesinje, the other municipality we used in the illustrations, there was no fighting of any sort. These were all towns that had been taken over by Serb forces, either before the war or very early in the war and the destruction happened subsequently, when the Serb authorities were firmly in control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you haven't established that any of these were used for military purposes, any of these structures; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't exclude the possibility, but I saw no evidence to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I shall talk collectively. You mention the institute for oriental studies, the library, the town hall in Sarajevo, Vijecnica. Do you have information that these facilities were used either as shelter or as firing positions by forces acting against Serb positions? Do you have any knowledge at all? Just give me a yes or no answer, please, because we don't have time.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I made inquiries, and as far as can be determined, neither the Oriental Institute nor the National Library were ever used by military forces. And if they had been, I would have expected allegation of this sort to surface during or immediately after the war, and they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you, then, as a matter of principle: Do you believe that the use of any of these sites for military purposes that were destroyed or damaged, would they be considered legitimate military targets in that case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Again, I'm not appearing as a legal expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. That's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you really believe that mosques, for instance, that were destroyed or damaged were destroyed or damaged because they were monuments of culture or in a war that also had a religious component to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you then give me an answer to the following question: If the intention of the Serbs, for instance, was to destroy certain cultural sites, why didn't they destroy the Hasanagica bridge in Trebinje, the Turkish towers over there, or the Mehmet Pasa Sokolovic bridge in Visegrad, another monument of culture, et cetera, et cetera? There are endless examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer why people didn't do it. You must ask them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that all these cultural sites which are sites of Muslim culture and which remained intact, that I have listed, in the places held by Bosnian Serb forces, is that evidence that they did not systematically destroy cultural heritage sites?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In the sites you have listed, like Trebinje and Visegrad, in fact all the mosques in town were destroyed. Why bridges were not singled out in the same way, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have also mentioned, for instance, the Turkish towers, which were not damaged either. So I'm talking about cultural monuments, not just bridges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness has answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that this destruction is a reflection of the religious component of the civil war that was being waged over there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't ask that question. It's been ruled out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that the Serbs who were destroying mosques knew which mosques are monuments of culture or part of the cultural heritage and which were not? Because one might ask: When they destroyed the mosque in Foca, why did they destroy it when it was known that it was built over the foundations of a Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: In Foca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't answer that. Well, if you can answer about Foca, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All I wanted to say is that in Foca, not only that mosque but every single mosque in the town, of which there were a considerable number - I think more than 20 in Foca and its suburbs - were all destroyed. I doubt that all of them were built over medieval churches, and I don't, for a fact, know that the Aladza mosque was built on a pre-existing church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You yourself say on page 10, paragraph 3, that almost 60 per cent of the mosques that were damaged or destroyed were built during Turkish rule. So does that mean that more than 40 per cent of the mosques in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were built during the existence of Yugoslavia, that is, a period of just over 70 years, almost half of the total number of mosques were built in the 70-year-long history of Yugoslavia, as compared to five centuries of Turkish rule.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This simply is a matter of what survives. The -- many of the new mosques were built to replace older mosques that had been damaged, for example, in earthquakes, in wars, or through ancient decrepitude. I think you would find very similar percentages in other parts of Europe of historic and modern buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard for me to choose. But if it is my last, then:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you write to your president, President Clinton in those days, Mr. Riedlmayer, asking him in your letter to lift the embargo on weapons deliveries to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was in the summer of 1995. And I had, you know, opinions about what was happening in the war in Bosnia, and my opinion was that under the United Nations charter the arms embargo violated the right of the -- the Bosnian government's right to self-defence. So yes, I did write that. But fact that I have engaged in political discourse does not, to my mind, affect my professional objectivity in reporting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, I would like to ask you to explain something to Their Honours with respect to the method you used in your work. I understood it - and I don't want to go back to that - that it was your job to ascertain the damages, according to the terms of reference, your terms of reference. Is that right? However, Mr. Riedlmayer, in your testimony today, when you were asked during the examination-in-chief, for example, you said that five mosques were destroyed in the course of one night, and then you went on to say that you knew or established something linked to the burning of the people in the mosque. Now, was that your job? Was it your job to delve into things that could be established in other ways? Wasn't it just your job to ascertain the damage done?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I considered it my job not only to do a physical description of what the condition of these buildings was as of the summer of 19 -- of 2002 but also insofar as possible find out why -- I mean, when they had been destroyed and how. One of the reasons is that I wanted to try to exclude as far as possible any buildings that had actually been destroyed before the war so as to limit it to war-damaged and war-destroyed buildings. Also, just as in my other report submitted to the Tribunal, while I did not go to great lengths to seek out and interview witnesses, if witnesses -- local witnesses were ready and forthcoming, I was in a position to simply write down what they stated. In the case of Bijeljina, it is not a matter open to question that five mosques were destroyed in a single night. It was widely reported at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Riedlmayer. But as my time is limited, I would like to know the following: In your written report, you used expressions of that kind: "To all intents and purposes," "perhaps," "it seems," "it would appear," and I can find examples of this but I don't think I need to do so at this point. But wasn't it necessary just to focus on the damage without making any assessments in using these kinds of terms? Because then it seems not that reliable for the Court to take this into consideration.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I was very careful, both in the database and in my summary report, to note what information I had on the basis of first-hand evidence and what information was either the result of conjecture on my part, drawing conclusions, or things which were reported to me. And so I used words like "reportedly" or "it appears" to indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to explain something now first. On the 30th of June, 2003, we received a lot of material pursuant to Rule 68. Of that multitude of material, referring to Mr. Riedlmayer - and this has direct bearing on the findings provided by Mr. Riedlmayer - I'd like to look at two documents and see if I'll have time for a third, to consider a third as well. May I look at two?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, the first document is an article by Matthew Battles, and -- "The Library." That's the title. Do you know about that article?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at page 4, paragraph 1 of that article, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it says there that Riedlmayer documented the damage and destruction of hundreds of other libraries, museums, and architectural heritage throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and in recent date Kosovo. And he's quoting you on that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes, he's summing up what I've written in numerous articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 4, please, paragraph 2, and here's what it says. It says that you stated - and he goes on to quote you - "Riedlmayer also considers - words that effect - that nationalist motives were more than obvious or evident throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. He wrote libraries archives, museums, and cultural institutions, they were the target of destruction in an effort to wipe out the material evidence, books, documents, and works of art, which could remind future generations that the peoples of different ethnic and religious traditions once shared the same heritage." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this nationalism that you're referring to here - because you don't mention any nation in particular - does it refer to all the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the nations?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I think it refers to all those who profess exclusivist nationalist ideologies, irrespective of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in that position taken by you, you don't differentiate between any of the nations living there. It refers to all of them, all the ethnic groups and nationalities living in the area.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I don't refer to nationalities; I refer to nationalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say, "Nationalist motives," that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can read that for ourselves in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would point out that the phrase "nationalist motive" is the author's words. The text that is attributed to Mr. Riedlmayer is in quotations and that particular portion of text is not in quotations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We do not have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give it back to Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you pay attention to this passage: It says, "Riedlmayer considers," and then it says what he considers. So it's not what the author says, it's what Riedlmayer says. That is my response to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But let's leave it to Their Honours to decide, not to belabour the point. I have another document here. It was disclosed to me on the 30th of June, 2003, pursuant to Rule 68, and it was published over the Internet. I don't have the ERN number of the OTP, but you yourself are the author of the article and it has to do with the Zitomislici monastery. I won't dwell on the Zitomislici monastery - you've already spoken about that - with respect to the document that was quoted, but not to disclose pursuant to Rule 68 but from this particular document, which you yourself wrote -- and here it is. I'll give you a copy of it. You say that "With respect to --"

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 5, paragraph 1. You say that in connection with the monastery that is being discussed, that you talked to the director of the museum of the Serbian Orthodox church, Mr. Slobodan Milevsic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I did not speak with him. I communicated with him through a third party, and he was kind enough to supply some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And now it goes on to say in the next paragraph that -- speaking about that, according to your information, which as you say comes from several sources, the Orthodox church was inflicted the greatest damages in the Neretva River Valley, when we take into account the territory of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And you refer to one of those sources -- or rather, the book written by Mr. Slobodan Milevsic, "Spiritual Genocide," is its title, as well as the report of Bishop Atanasije, the bishop of Herzegovina. I'm sure you've had the book. You've seen the book.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to conclude on this point, if we are able to clarify it. And I must say that in the short space of time it was thanks to the bishop of Banja Luka, Mr. Jefrem Milutinovic, that I was able to come by the book that you had in your possession. Is this the book? Is this it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I have an earlier edition of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the book, please. Page 234, where you'll find this map and the facts or, rather, information as to the number of churches and other structures which were destroyed from 1991 to 1995, and they even mention a figure of 797 and 212 churches completely destroyed. Do you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: First of all, as I indicated, what I had was the earlier edition of this, which did not have the map or that number, for that matter. What I do recall from looking at the book is that while it includes a lot more photographs than the other book that was cited, it is also not terribly careful in keeping apart allegations of World War II damage and allegations of damage during the war.
