So I can't confirm this 797. The 797, as I see, also includes 212 churches alleged to have been destroyed, 367 alleged to have been damaged. As I say, I have no way of confirming that figure, seeing as I haven't done a systematic study on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If your lords please, it's first of all I'd just like to say the Prosecution takes no objection to the exhibited photographs of the book, largely on the grounds that they're not charged in the indictment as destroyed Serbian property, so we're quite happy for them to remain. I just have a couple of questions to ask the witness in re-examination, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, there's been a lot of discussion and questions as to what amounts to cultural property and heritage. Now, in your view, can buildings, land, or other things amount to cultural property or be a part of a country's heritage even if it's not listed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, in your view, would it be correct that those religious sites, libraries, and archives, mentioned in your report, would all amount to being a part of the religious cultural heritage of the Bosnian people?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, having clarified that point, another point which the accused again raised and which there were many questions was this concept of the religious property mentioned in your report being destroyed by each side mutually during war, tit for tat, if you like. Now, obviously based on your research, the evidence you've gathered, and the witnesses you've spoken to, would you think that is a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, what are your grounds for saying this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: A number of things: Typically, when you have acts of retribution taking place, they tend to be spontaneous acts, involving, for example -- the typical example would be a group of expelled people returns to their village, finds their house of worship destroyed, those who destroyed it have left, and so they, you know, turn their vengeance and their anger upon the physical symbols of those whom they blame for their own suffering. So that is a very typical kind of destruction. Generally, the kind of tit for tat thing also tends to be sporadic. It depends on circumstances and opportunity. So the one thing that speaks against it is the systematic and uniform nature of the destruction that I saw and documented. The second one is the fact that much of this destruction occurred not in the heat of conflict, but at times when the areas in question were under control of the Bosnian Serb authorities, which suggests, along with other factors that I mentioned, such as the use of explosives and the amount of organisation involved, which suggests that this was not merely a matter of mob anger but of some sort of directed policy. And lastly, if you had a real tit for tat relationship, one could expect the same pattern and degree of destruction on all sides. And as I've explained, this is clearly not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, just two very particular questions on this: Is it correct that to a large degree a majority of the religious sites you mentioned in your report were destroyed whilst there was no fighting going on in their vicinity?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: That is certainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And would it also be correct from the sites you visited and other evidence you gathered, photographic and so on, that in many instances the mosques or other religious property appeared to be targeted on account of the surrounding buildings being untouched?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Not only the question of the context of the surrounding buildings being untouched. Very often you can judge this from the method of destruction. For example, a very common way of destroying a mosque or a church steeple was to place explosives within it. You can establish that this happens by various factors. The structure balloons outward as a result of the explosion. You can see radiating scorch marks, all kinds of evidence. Although I'm not a military expert, at this point I have probably seen several hundred such destroyed structures and can base my conclusions on that experience. Now, it seems to me that it is very unlikely that such a thing would happen in the context of a military conflict, just to dislodge a sniper or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Okay. Very briefly now, if I may, on a slightly different area. The accused produced earlier a letter, which I believe has been marked for identification. It wasn't actually in the English language. And that letter, I believe, concerned the order for security forces to guard mosques and religious buildings to a greater extent because they may be under attack in Banja Luka. Now, can you remember the date of the letter that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Perhaps we could be reminded. D159, I'm informed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The date of the letter is 12 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, at that time, were there any mosques still standing in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: There were several mosques still standing. At that point, three had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did there remain -- did they remain standing or ...?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: The other 13 were destroyed in the succeeding months. By December of 1993, not a single mosque was left in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Okay. So despite this order which was clearly ignored and the extra security that the mosques were destroyed totally in Banja Luka -- and are you aware of anyone being prosecuted for that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: You're not. Now, I just have two final questions for you. I'm trying to keep this brief. The first is: Are you aware of St. Sava's church in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Is that church completed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: No. It's been under construction for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And do -- does a congregation gather there for services?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes. It's used.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And that being a part-built structure, church --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: -- Would you regard that as being religious and cultural property?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: I would believe so. It's been used, among other things, for memorial services for the late Prime Minister Djindjic recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if you were so instructed to carry out a similar survey in respect of damage to Serbian cultural property in Bosnia, would you be prepared to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And just finally, the last question I have for you is that Judge Robinson asked you if you could possibly put a monetary value on the destruction of all the religious property in Bosnia. Is there anything that springs to your mind that any witness may have mentioned to you concerning the value of that destroyed property to them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: Well, that springs to -- brings to mind the question of what value is in a nonmonetary sense. Consider in a village the local house of worship even for people who are not actively religious. It is the site where their parents and grandparents may have been buried. It is the single visible reminder of the community's presence in that locality. And it is also a major investment by the community, getting together to build such a thing. So an attack on such a monument is more than just material damage. It is -- it wounds the sensibility of the entire community. And as I mention in my report, for the people who did this, it was very clear what such destruction meant. You know, the police chief in Prijedor was interviewed by a Western reporter and asked about it, and this is the late Simo Drljaca, who was appointed by Radovan Karadzic as regional police chief for Prijedor and five other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness. Which page of your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER
utterances.text: This is page 12 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Does the Chamber have this, page 12?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so he says: "With their mosques you must not just break the minarets," he said. "You've got to shake up the foundations because that means they cannot build another. Do that, and they'll want to go. They'll just leave by themselves." And similarly the victims were very conscious of this. And I can cite you one statement from my database here. This is -- just a moment. Yeah. Okay. Yes, this is a statement quoted by Tim Juda reporting from Banja Luka on the 14th of May, 1993 after the sixteenth century Ferhadija mosque had been blown up. Said one Muslim onlooker, "It is as though they have torn our heart out. They wanted us to understand that we have no place here." And that is, I submit, the statement as to what the value of these objects was.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for returning to the Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness -- before the next witness, I request that the next witness be brought in, there is the matter of protective measures. If we could go into private session to discuss these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Ambassador Edhem Pasic. Your Honour, could I just advise the Chamber that before we adjourn today, if it's possible, there are about three or four minutes' worth of procedural matters I would like to raise with the Chamber. If I may ask the registrar to distribute the proofing summary and the single exhibit while we are waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ambassador Pasic, after a ruling by the Court, we will be proceeding in open session and addressing you by your name. If there's any portion of the testimony that you feel should be taken in closed session because of security concerns, please advise me and I will make that request of the Chamber. I'd ask you to begin your testimony by describing for us your current position.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I am now Ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Kuwait.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long have you held that post?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: For two and a half years, about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And your presence here at the Tribunal today, is that in an official capacity or as a private citizen that has relevant information for this trial?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I am not here today in an official capacity. I am here in my own behalf and in the name of all of us in the south of Europe who wish to lead a normal life without discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now back to the early 1990s. Can you describe what position you held during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, I was editor of the office for Arabic, Turkish, and Chinese languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when did you begin such work?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I started performing that duty in 1977, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when did you finish or complete that work?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I stopped performing those duties de facto already in 1991/1992, de facto. But de jure, I remained in that position until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you for a further explanation of that answer, I'm going to ask that the witness be shown a document, and I'd ask that it be assigned a number at this time. It is the only exhibit that will be tendered through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P489.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, is that a summary of your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your last answer to my question -- to my last question, you said that there was -- there was a change in how you perceived your role. Could I first ask you to identify the time period during which you perceived this change, and then please explain the change.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The changes occurred when the changes happened in the Yugoslavia of the day. Those changes could be felt immediately after the eighth session. There was a cleansing of all personnel that were not considered politically suitable, not just non-Serbs but also Serbs that were not loyal to the new course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you see such personnel changes among Serb co-workers and colleagues in the departments that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. It's not clear to me to this day how many people suddenly changed. There was such a campaign of the public opinion, propaganda, the media, that people only spoke about what was coming from the headquarters of the now-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you yourself demoted during this time period?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I was. I was returned back to the beginning. I had the post of an ordinary translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when was that? When were you demoted?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: As far as I can now remember, this was between 1991 and 1992. And I was informed at the time that the plan had been to remove me from that position. But as I said in my statement, fortunately I had quite a lot of friends. One of my friends then had a very senior position in the federal administration, and he protected me so that I could retain formally the position I held until I fled from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when was it that you fled from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the period of 1991 and 1994, was your apartment in Belgrade ever subject to searches?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently. My wife and I would leave certain things to be able to tell when we returned that the flat had been searched. And as there were a lot of books in my apartment, especially in the oriental languages that I speak, many of those books simply disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time during the early 1990s when you were required to go to briefings conducted by the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in an atmosphere - not just I, but all of us who were in the same position - an atmosphere of terrible fear. I was asked, but I never learned who those people were. They were always wearing plain clothes. I never knew their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And on how many occasions were you required to meet with these people?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Very frequently, very frequently. They would intercept me in public places sometimes. Usually this was on a Monday. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what would happen when these people would approach you?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: What would happen was that they would always caution me, because I was working at confidential activities in the former Yugoslavia, as they said, and that they wouldn't let me go, having state secrets in my mind, that they wanted to keep me there under their control and that I mustn't tell anyone about these requests made of me, not even my wife. And I informed my wife about it only once we reached Cairo, when I had fled from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention now to the summer of 1992. During that time period, did you have occasion to be in the office of the then-president, Dobrica Cosic?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I did. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he was the federal president at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the purpose of your presence at his office.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Before I came to his office, some people came and told me that two presidents wanted me to assist in a telephone conversation they were due to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who were they to have this telephone conversation with?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: It was a telephone conversation between the leader of Libya, Moammar Gadhafi, and the then-president of the federal Yugoslavia, Mr. Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know why you were asked to assist in this telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But people I knew from before in Cosic's office, that most probably Gadhafi, whom I had known, asked me to interpret because I had interpreted frequently when he came to visit Yugoslavia and vice versa, when the highest level officials of the former Yugoslavia went to visit Libya.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you went to President Cosic's office, were you required to wait for some period of time before you were able to assist in this manner?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We waited a long time. Because to establish the telephone connection between Tripoli and Belgrade took a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you approximate how long you waited before becoming involved in the telephone call?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect now, I think it was close to an hour, maybe more, maybe less, but approximately that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While you were waiting in the president's office, were there other people in the office waiting as well?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: There were. The then-federal Minister of Foreign Affairs was present, Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Besides Mr. Jovanovic, were there any other people present in the office?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: The office is a big one. People were coming and going. But as far as I can recollect now, also present from time to time was the then-deputy of the chief of cabinet of President Dobrica Cosic, whom I knew from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers in the office?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: In the office, I didn't see any soldiers, but there were a lot of soldiers in the corridors, in the anterooms, when I was arriving, before I entered this room where I was waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the condition of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: They had different uniforms and insignia from the so-called Republic of Krajina - that is how it was called, I think - and also from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to hear any of the conversations of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDHEM PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them. I heard those conversations before entering this waiting room. They were talking about battlefronts that they were coming from. Some of them had mud on their clothes even. And I remember that a group who wore an emblem saying that it was a Cyrillic -- I think it was in Cyrillic, the word "brigade." I think that was so, but I couldn't see too well. It was quite dark in the corridor. And while I was waiting to enter the waiting room, I heard some conversation about killings in Bosnian villages, slaughters, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to embark on a rather lengthy portion of the witness's testimony. Would this be a convenient place to break for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. Ambassador, we're going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning. Could you remember over the break not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. That's the warning we give all witnesses, of course. And could you be back, please, tomorrow morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness go. There are one or two matters which Mr. Groome wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first is the matter of Ambassador Okun. If I could remind the Court, he completed his cross-examination some time ago, and all that remained were for some questions to be put to him by the amici. I've spoken with Mr. Kay earlier about how to proceed. If you recall, the Chamber had suggested that possibly it was a matter that could be dealt with by simply putting written questions to Ambassador Okun and that he would respond to. It had been planned to bring him back around this time period because it was believed that he would be testifying in another case. That case has been indefinitely adjourned and it does not appear that it will begin before the Prosecution case concludes here. I've spoken with Mr. Kay about it, and he is amenable, if the Court still is, to presenting to Ambassador Okun some written questions, receiving back a written reply, and then evaluating at that time whether it's actually necessary to actually go through the expense to have Ambassador Okun come back to the chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. As the opportunity no longer presents itself for him to return, there were five issues I was going to raise with him, which would have taken only 15 minutes. But it would be the best way to proceed in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second matter, Your Honour, is next Monday the Prosecution had intended to call Witness Nenad Zafirovic. A problem has arisen regarding his ability to travel, and it is a problem that we cannot resolve prior to the -- the summer break. So I would just notify the Chamber, the accused, and the amici that he will not be here next Monday. We will be advancing the witnesses later in that week up until Monday. And similarly, there may be a difficulty with respect to Witness B-150, who was scheduled to testify this Friday, that -- I cannot give definite word yet, but I do want to give the Chamber, the accused, and the amici as early notice as possible there may be some difficulty with his testifying this coming Friday. And again, we will be advancing some of the 92 bis witnesses that had been scheduled for next week to make the best use of the court time. That concludes the points I want to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Tomorrow morning, 9.00, when we will expect - is that right - Mr. Lilic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So Mr. Milosevic, first thing tomorrow morning Mr. Lilic. Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
